Say I have 100 landmarks: 20 define curve1, 40 define curve 2, 40 define curve3. I know how to use digit.curves to get the start/end and evenly spaced coords for each segment.

Assuming I have 50 images, all with the same landmarks defining the same curves etc., how would I batch process all of them at the same time? I know I'd read in my TPS file, but how to go from 100 raw LMs to the three sets of spaced LMs with all specimens in a single tps file.

Thanks in advance!
Russ

messages.subject: GM Workshop: Glasgow, October 2019
messages.body_plain:
>From Oliver Hooker, PR Statistics:

Workshop: Geometric morphometrics using (Geomorph) R
	14th - 18th October 2019 in Glasgow City Centre

https://www.prstatistics.com/course/geometric-morphometrics-using-r-gmmr02/

This course will be delivered by Prof. Dean Adams, Prof Mike Collyer and Dr. Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou form the 14th - 18th October 2019 in Glasgow City Centre.

Course overview:
The field of geometric morphometrics (GM) is concerned with the quantification and analysis of patterns of shape variation, and its covariation with other variables. Over the past several decades these approaches have become a mainstay in the field of ecology, evolutionary biology, and anthropology, and a panoply of analytical tools for addressing specific biological hypotheses concerning shape have been developed. The goal of this is to provide participants with a working knowledge of the theory of geometric morphometrics, as well as practical training in the application of these methods.

The course is organized in both theoretical and practical sessions.
The theoretical sessions will provide a comprehensive introduction to the methods of landmark-based geometric morphometrics, which aims at providing the participants with a solid theoretical background for understanding the procedures used in shape data analysis. Practical sessions will include worked examples, giving the participants the opportunity to gain hands-on experience in the treatment of shape data using the R package geomorph. These sessions focus on the generation of shape variables from primary landmark data, the statistical treatment of shape variation with respect to biological hypotheses, and the visualization of patterns of shape variation and of the shapes themselves for interpretation of statistical findings, using the R language for statistical programming. While practice datasets will be available, it is strongly recommended that participants come with their own datasets.

Note: Because this is a geometric morphometrics workshop in R, it is assumed, and is in fact required, that participants have some working knowledge in R. The practical sessions of the course will focus on GM-based analyses, and not basic R user-interfacing. It is therefore strongly recommended that participants refresh their R skills prior to attending the workshop.

Email oliver...@prstatistics.com

messages.subject: to mshape or to not mshape
messages.subject_clean: to mshape or to not mshape
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I’m analysing stomata from an evergreen tree species along and altitudinal gradient. So far, I have collected 2D landmarks for 320 stomata (32 leaves, 10 stomata per leaf).

I have already performed simple allometry model and evaluate HOS converting altitude to a three-way factor (low, middle and high). Both Csize and faltitude seem to have a significant effect in the shape variation of stomata, and altitude groups have common allometry. However, I’m unsure if it would be better idea running the analysis based on mshape of stomata per leaf within altitude groups, mainly because I have measure 10 stomata (replicates) per leaf, and perhaps, I could use it to understand stomatal shape variation within leaves or measurement error.

I would also like to incorporate in my analysis other variables I have measured such as, mean stomatal density, mean stomatal index, mean leaf area, and environmental variables (e.g. mean annual temperature). and here, I think, is where the mshape of  per leaf could come in handy. Any advice will be greatly appreciate.

Thanks in advance,

Giselle

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] to mshape or to not mshape
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] to mshape or to not mshape
messages.body_plain:
Giselle,

You have to be careful because you also probably have size variation among stomata both within and across leaves that you do not want to disregard when finding means.  I would recommend - because common allometry can be assumed - that you find allometry-free shapes before getting means.  Here is an example for how to do that:

res <- prcoD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize), data = mydata, iter = 1)$residuals # removing allometry
means <- prcoD.lm(coords ~ 1, data = mydata, iter = 1)$fitted # overall mean shape
Y.adj <- mean + res # These are shapes with allometry removed
mydata$coords.adj <- arrayspecs(Y.adj, p, k) # using p = number of landmarks and k = 2 for 2D data

Then you could use mshape by leaf to get leaf mean shapes on coords.adj.  This way, if you have a leaf with many large stomata or many small stomata, you are estimating the mean shape of the leaf as if it has the average sized stomata, like all other leaves.

I agree that the leaf is a better research subject than the individual, repeated measures on each leaf.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
David and the group,

This is an interesting case. Essentially, the multiple aspects of symmetry in the shapes are confusing the PLS algorithm. This can happen, but having a way to catch it is hard.

However, this example emphasizes an important point: landmark estimation really needs to be used NOT as a black box, but rather with frequent inspection of the estimated shapes; as David has done here. In many cases, the PLS-regression is generally better, but not always. This is a case of the not always.

Dean

messages.subject: digit.curves - Equidistant semilandmarks in 3D
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph-community,

finished recently my 2D-project I now go on with 3D data sets and promptly face a problem^^

I digitize three 3D curves on CT surfaces of several specimens and export them as Morphologika-format (with Checkpoint). Further, some fixed landmarks are included. Data is present as array in R with dim(data) = 63,3,3. Here, only three specimens are included for a trial. Latter there will be over 100.

The three curves were digitized always with the same amount of points namely 21,6 and 29 points. These points are yet not equally distributed along the curves, which I want now to do in geomorph with digit.curves.

First, I split the raw data into datasets inlcuding only the fixed LM´s and each curve separately and latter on, after placing equidistant semiLM, bind them together again with "abind()", as I found our already. The problem is now how to do the equidistant semiLM with 3D data with several specimens at once? In the Users guide of geomorph there is only an example for a single LM configuration in 2D. Just following it to try whether it works also with matrices does not work out.
So far, I am still far away in being an expert in R. I suggest one would need some kind of a loop-function to do this, defining always the next starting point of the curve for the next specimen in row.
I hope I gave you all information you need and you can help me with that problem :D

Thank you in advance!
Peter

Skript so far:

filelist<-list.files(pattern="*.txt")
data<-read.morphologika(filelist)                           #reads in all morphologika-files in the filelist into one 3D array
dimnames(data)[[3]] <- gsub (".txt", "", filelist)        #adds specimen name to array from file name

#separate fixed landmarks form semilandmarks

curve1<-curves[c(1:21),,]

curve3<-curves[c(28:56),,]

###place equidistant semilandmarks for each curve
#curve1
c1<-two.d.array(curve1)     #converting to matrix

???? This does not work out ????

start1<-c1[,1:3]
lmks<-digit.curves(start1,c1,nPoints=12,closed=F)            # curve1 is build with 21 points, nPoints < 21

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] digit.curves - Equidistant semilandmarks in 3D
messages.body_plain:
Peter,

If you are happy with the Morpho/equidistant function, I would stick with it, but here is why I think, as a philosophy, a similar function in geomorph would be dangerous.  The digit.curves function works by sampling a set pf p < P points, where p is the desired number and P is full set of points in the curve, perhaps from an automated curve-defining function, like can be found in Stereomorph.  If one attempts to define p, when p = P or p > P, it should not work because there are too few points from which to sample.

It appears the equidistant function will generate points that hypothetically exist between digitized points to inflate P so that p can be sampled, as if these new points precisely fall on the actual curve (I could be misinterpreting the code - I did not try to fully pick it apart).  This might work well in some cases (many points not too far apart) but could be disastrous in others (create points that could not physically exist on a specimen).

Regarding your specific case, even when p < P, yes you have to make a loop, as digit.curves is a specimen-specific function.  The directions indicate that each specimen has to be a p x k matrix of points.  You used two.d.array, which makes each specimen a 1 x (p*k) vector of points.  This will not work.

There are various ways to do a loop; here’s one:

myCurves <- lapply(1:n, function(j) {

x <- coords[,,j]
digit.cuves(x, start, end, …)

})

where n is the number of specimens, coords is generic for the coords to use, in a 3D array, and the rest should be obvious.

This will create a list but the list can be converted to an array with simplify2array.

Hope that helps.
Mike

messages.subject_clean: Functions digit.fixed, build template and digitsurface no longer work for me since updating R and RStudio
messages.body_plain:
Hi geomorph community,

This is my firs post to the community. I'm using geomorph to digitize fixed and semi-landmarks on juvenile clavicles to capture changes in clavicular shape.

Here is my code to digitize my fixed and semi-landmarks:

### NP075LClavicle is a Mesh 3D object
fixed.LeftNP075 <- digit.fixed(spec = NP075LClavicle, fixed = 7, index = FALSE, ptsize = 1, center = TRUE)
semi.LeftNP075 <- buildtemplate(spec = NP075LClavicle, fixed = fixed.LeftNP075, surface.sliders = 100)
digitsurface(spec = NP075LClavicle, fixed = fixed.LeftNP075)

Previously, I never had an issue with this code. However, since updating to the latest version of both R and Rstudio, this code no longer works. I now encounter the following error message with both digit.fixed and digitsurface: "Error: $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors".

I believe this errors is arising from my Mesh 3D object, but I'm not sure.

Why is this error occurring and how can I fixed it?

Thanks,
Sean

messages.subject: Strange use of covariates in pairwise()
messages.subject_clean: Strange use of covariates in pairwise()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I think I've run into a strange issue using the pairwise function in RRPP to compare angles of vectors, and I was just wondering if you had any idea of what is going on here.

Basically, I was just running a pairwise test with a single response variable, a single factor, and a continuous covariate to see how it compared to a regular ANCOVA.  I don't have a null model, because I am just interested in the angles between factor levels.  The problem is that all the angles of the group vectors were either 0º or 180º to each other, so the covariate seemed to be acting like another factor, not a continuous variable.  This isn't a huge issue in this instance because I can just use an ANCOVA, but I am also worried it is doing something similar with shape data, but it is difficult to tell since the response is multivariate.

Do you have any clue what is going on here or how to fix it?

The code I have is something like this:

rrpp.df<-rrpp.data.frame(X1,X2,Y)
lm<-lm.rrpp(data = rrpp.df, Y~X1*X2)
PW<-pairwise(lm, groups = X1, covariate = X2)
summary(PW, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC", angle.type = "deg")

thanks in advance,
Grant

messages.body_plain:
Grant,

You are attempting to find the angle between vectors on a line.  Vectors have both a length and a direction in space with two dimensions (plane) or more, but on a line, you lose direction except for “forward” and “backward”, i.e., 0 and 180 degrees, respectively.

It is not a strange issue with RRPP/pairwise; it’s a strange test to test the angle between vectors on a line.  The only test that can make sense is the distance between means or slopes on that line, in which case the pairwise test becomes a non-parametric form of univariate tests for pairwise differences in means or slopes, respectively.  In other words, use test.type = “dist”, only, in the summary for univariate data.

The last paragraph of the help file explains this (although a typo of test.type = ‘cor’ instead of test.type = ‘VC’ might cause some confusion - the text should still be clear about why a vector correlation does not make sense).

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Ian,

Yes, the purpose seems clear, but there is not a vector of coefficients.  You have scalars b1 and b2 for two groups because there is only one variable for Y.  If b1 and b2 were vectors, you could find the distance between them and the angle between them.  As scalars, there is only a distance between them, as they exist on a line.

In most classic univariate statistics texts/instructional sources, one might learn with ANCOVA that a pairwise comparison of slopes is performed with t = |b1 - b2|/se (using absolute values for simplicity).  That numerator is the same as the distance statistic in the RRPP pairwise summary.  The test is testing for differences between slopes, because the covariate was defined.  But slope vectors can differ in both magnitude and direction (e.g., the amount of shape change per unit size and the direction of shape change per unit size) unless there is only one variable, in which case the amount of Y change per unit size change is all one can assess.

The only issue here is that the RRPP/pairwise function returns a result instead of alerting the user that a result like that should not be sought.  The latter is much more complicated from a programming perspective than trying to explain it in the help file, or this forum.

I hope that makes sense.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
This was the presentation:

>
> > > > Basically, I was just running a pairwise test with a single response variable, a single factor, ...
> > >

As a simple demonstration, Grant could make Y a two-variable response and everything would change.

Cheers!
Mike

> On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:57 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Mike and Grant,
>
>  Was his response a single variable? I assumed because he used Y not y in his notation,  it was a vector of multiple response variables.
>
> On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 09:56, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Ian,
> >
> > Yes, the purpose seems clear, but there is not a vector of coefficients.  You have scalars b1 and b2 for two groups because there is only one variable for Y.  If b1 and b2 were vectors, you could find the distance between them and the angle between them.  As scalars, there is only a distance between them, as they exist on a line.
> >
> > In most classic univariate statistics texts/instructional sources, one might learn with ANCOVA that a pairwise comparison of slopes is performed with t = |b1 - b2|/se (using absolute values for simplicity).  That numerator is the same as the distance statistic in the RRPP pairwise summary.  The test is testing for differences between slopes, because the covariate was defined.  But slope vectors can differ in both magnitude and direction (e.g., the amount of shape change per unit size and the direction of shape change per unit size) unless there is only one variable, in which case the amount of Y change per unit size change is all one can assess.
> >
> > The only issue here is that the RRPP/pairwise function returns a result instead of alerting the user that a result like that should not be sought.  The latter is much more complicated from a programming perspective than trying to explain it in the help file, or this forum.
> >
> > I hope that makes sense.
> >
> > Mike
> >
> > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:44 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Mike (and Grant),
> > >
> > >  If I understand correctly what Grant is trying to achieve is to compare the angle between the vector of coefficients from the model Y ~ X2 between the groups defined by X1. i.e. like comparing the vector of coefficients from a model of shape on size for two groups (say males and females), and comparing the angle between the allometry vectors.
> > >
> > > Let me know if I misunderstood the question.
> > >
> > > Also we have code (probably also available in geomorph, since it seems to do everything now!) to generate CI on the angle or vector correlation via np-bootstrap. Let me know if that is useful.
> > >
> > > On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 09:29, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Grant,
> > > >
> > > > You are attempting to find the angle between vectors on a line.  Vectors have both a length and a direction in space with two dimensions (plane) or more, but on a line, you lose direction except for “forward” and “backward”, i.e., 0 and 180 degrees, respectively.
> > > >
> > > > It is not a strange issue with RRPP/pairwise; it’s a strange test to test the angle between vectors on a line.  The only test that can make sense is the distance between means or slopes on that line, in which case the pairwise test becomes a non-parametric form of univariate tests for pairwise differences in means or slopes, respectively.  In other words, use test.type = “dist”, only, in the summary for univariate data.
> > > >
> > > > The last paragraph of the help file explains this (although a typo of test.type = ‘cor’ instead of test.type = ‘VC’ might cause some confusion - the text should still be clear about why a vector correlation does not make sense).
> > > >
> > > > Mike
> > > >
> > > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:14 AM, Grant Haines <geha...@email.wm.edu> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi all,
> > > > >
> > > > > I think I've run into a strange issue using the pairwise function in RRPP to compare angles of vectors, and I was just wondering if you had any idea of what is going on here.
> > > > >
> > > > > Basically, I was just running a pairwise test with a single response variable, a single factor, and a continuous covariate to see how it compared to a regular ANCOVA.  I don't have a null model, because I am just interested in the angles between factor levels.  The problem is that all the angles of the group vectors were either 0º or 180º to each other, so the covariate seemed to be acting like another factor, not a continuous variable.  This isn't a huge issue in this instance because I can just use an ANCOVA, but I am also worried it is doing something similar with shape data, but it is difficult to tell since the response is multivariate.
> > > > >
> > > > > Do you have any clue what is going on here or how to fix it?
> > > > >
> > > > > The code I have is something like this:
> > > > >
> > > > > rrpp.df<-rrpp.data.frame(X1,X2,Y)
> > > > > lm<-lm.rrpp(data = rrpp.df, Y~X1*X2)
> > > > > PW<-pairwise(lm, groups = X1, covariate = X2)
> > > > > summary(PW, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC", angle.type = "deg")
> > > > >
> > > > > thanks in advance,
> > > > > Grant

messages.body_plain:
No worries - a good discussion for the forum, as it might not be intuitive.

For everyone listening, traditionally, when a pairwise slope test for univariate data reveals a significant difference in slopes, it can be said, “the angle between slopes is significantly different”.  This is true, as it means the “rise” for one group over an interval of “run” for both groups is higher or lower, compared to the other.  This construct creates a plane for interpretation fo univariate data.  Thus, a > 1D data space - where slope vectors are vectors comprising several scalars, not just one scalar - would analogously require a 3D+ space to also include “run” for interpretation.  We generally do not do that -  we just work in the data space - but run exists in that space as a distance along the slope vector.  I like to think of shape change vectors colored blue, for example, and we can color code a portion of those blue vectors as red, corresponding to one unit of size change.  If one vector has a larger red segment than another, the distance option for comparison might reveal the two groups are different in the amount of allometric shape change.  Coloring the vectors red does nothing to change their orientation, so the angle between these vectors is a distinct test.

The problem is the word, “angle”, has different meanings in the two interpretations.  I try to refrain from using “angle between slopes” for univariate data and make sure to say “different slopes” so that “angle” is a property of a multivariate space, only.  But it is confusing, nonetheless.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Grant,

Including a covariate means you are comparing slope vectors among groups; not including one means you are comapring least squares means among groups.

Mike

> On Jul 10, 2019, at 3:36 PM, Grant Haines <geha...@email.wm.edu> wrote:
>

> Hi Ian and Mike,
>
> Thanks very much for the responses, and sorry I wasn't able to get back to this earlier today.  This does clear up the language you are using quite a bit.
>
> I just tried running a similar model with a bivariate response variable with and without the covariate, and I think I understand a bit better.  The angles do change when the covariate is included, though, which I have a hard time making sense of in the context of your above statement about the orientation of the vectors not changing.
>
> cheers,
> Grant
>
> On Wed, Jul 10, 2019 at 10:51 AM Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > No worries - a good discussion for the forum, as it might not be intuitive.
> >
> > For everyone listening, traditionally, when a pairwise slope test for univariate data reveals a significant difference in slopes, it can be said, “the angle between slopes is significantly different”.  This is true, as it means the “rise” for one group over an interval of “run” for both groups is higher or lower, compared to the other.  This construct creates a plane for interpretation fo univariate data.  Thus, a > 1D data space - where slope vectors are vectors comprising several scalars, not just one scalar - would analogously require a 3D+ space to also include “run” for interpretation.  We generally do not do that -  we just work in the data space - but run exists in that space as a distance along the slope vector.  I like to think of shape change vectors colored blue, for example, and we can color code a portion of those blue vectors as red, corresponding to one unit of size change.  If one vector has a larger red segment than another, the distance option for comparison might reveal the two groups are different in the amount of allometric shape change.  Coloring the vectors red does nothing to change their orientation, so the angle between these vectors is a distinct test.
> >
> > The problem is the word, “angle”, has different meanings in the two interpretations.  I try to refrain from using “angle between slopes” for univariate data and make sure to say “different slopes” so that “angle” is a property of a multivariate space, only.  But it is confusing, nonetheless.
> >
> > Cheers!
> > Mike
> >
> > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 10:04 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Mike,
> > >
> > >  Whoops my bad, I just looked at the notation!
> > >
> > > On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 10:02, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > This was the presentation:
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > > > > Basically, I was just running a pairwise test with a single response variable, a single factor, ...
> > > > > > >
> > > >
> > > > As a simple demonstration, Grant could make Y a two-variable response and everything would change.
> > > >
> > > > Cheers!
> > > > Mike
> > > >
> > > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:57 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Mike and Grant,
> > > > >
> > > > >  Was his response a single variable? I assumed because he used Y not y in his notation,  it was a vector of multiple response variables.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 09:56, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Ian,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Yes, the purpose seems clear, but there is not a vector of coefficients.  You have scalars b1 and b2 for two groups because there is only one variable for Y.  If b1 and b2 were vectors, you could find the distance between them and the angle between them.  As scalars, there is only a distance between them, as they exist on a line.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In most classic univariate statistics texts/instructional sources, one might learn with ANCOVA that a pairwise comparison of slopes is performed with t = |b1 - b2|/se (using absolute values for simplicity).  That numerator is the same as the distance statistic in the RRPP pairwise summary.  The test is testing for differences between slopes, because the covariate was defined.  But slope vectors can differ in both magnitude and direction (e.g., the amount of shape change per unit size and the direction of shape change per unit size) unless there is only one variable, in which case the amount of Y change per unit size change is all one can assess.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The only issue here is that the RRPP/pairwise function returns a result instead of alerting the user that a result like that should not be sought.  The latter is much more complicated from a programming perspective than trying to explain it in the help file, or this forum.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I hope that makes sense.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Mike
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:44 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Mike (and Grant),
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >  If I understand correctly what Grant is trying to achieve is to compare the angle between the vector of coefficients from the model Y ~ X2 between the groups defined by X1. i.e. like comparing the vector of coefficients from a model of shape on size for two groups (say males and females), and comparing the angle between the allometry vectors.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Let me know if I misunderstood the question.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Also we have code (probably also available in geomorph, since it seems to do everything now!) to generate CI on the angle or vector correlation via np-bootstrap. Let me know if that is useful.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 09:29, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > Grant,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > You are attempting to find the angle between vectors on a line.  Vectors have both a length and a direction in space with two dimensions (plane) or more, but on a line, you lose direction except for “forward” and “backward”, i.e., 0 and 180 degrees, respectively.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > It is not a strange issue with RRPP/pairwise; it’s a strange test to test the angle between vectors on a line.  The only test that can make sense is the distance between means or slopes on that line, in which case the pairwise test becomes a non-parametric form of univariate tests for pairwise differences in means or slopes, respectively.  In other words, use test.type = “dist”, only, in the summary for univariate data.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > The last paragraph of the help file explains this (although a typo of test.type = ‘cor’ instead of test.type = ‘VC’ might cause some confusion - the text should still be clear about why a vector correlation does not make sense).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Mike
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:14 AM, Grant Haines <geha...@email.wm.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Hi all,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I think I've run into a strange issue using the pairwise function in RRPP to compare angles of vectors, and I was just wondering if you had any idea of what is going on here.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Basically, I was just running a pairwise test with a single response variable, a single factor, and a continuous covariate to see how it compared to a regular ANCOVA.  I don't have a null model, because I am just interested in the angles between factor levels.  The problem is that all the angles of the group vectors were either 0º or 180º to each other, so the covariate seemed to be acting like another factor, not a continuous variable.  This isn't a huge issue in this instance because I can just use an ANCOVA, but I am also worried it is doing something similar with shape data, but it is difficult to tell since the response is multivariate.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Do you have any clue what is going on here or how to fix it?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The code I have is something like this:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > rrpp.df<-rrpp.data.frame(X1,X2,Y)
> > > > > > > > > lm<-lm.rrpp(data = rrpp.df, Y~X1*X2)
> > > > > > > > > PW<-pairwise(lm, groups = X1, covariate = X2)
> > > > > > > > > summary(PW, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC", angle.type = "deg")
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > thanks in advance,
> > > > > > > > > Grant

messages.body_plain:
Got it, thanks again for clearing this up.

Grant

On Wed, Jul 10, 2019 at 3:55 PM Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Grant,
>
> Including a covariate means you are comparing slope vectors among groups; not including one means you are comapring least squares means among groups.
>
> Mike
>
> > On Jul 10, 2019, at 3:36 PM, Grant Haines <geha...@email.wm.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Ian and Mike,
> >
> > Thanks very much for the responses, and sorry I wasn't able to get back to this earlier today.  This does clear up the language you are using quite a bit.
> >
> > I just tried running a similar model with a bivariate response variable with and without the covariate, and I think I understand a bit better.  The angles do change when the covariate is included, though, which I have a hard time making sense of in the context of your above statement about the orientation of the vectors not changing.
> >
> > cheers,
> > Grant
> >
> > On Wed, Jul 10, 2019 at 10:51 AM Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > No worries - a good discussion for the forum, as it might not be intuitive.
> > >
> > > For everyone listening, traditionally, when a pairwise slope test for univariate data reveals a significant difference in slopes, it can be said, “the angle between slopes is significantly different”.  This is true, as it means the “rise” for one group over an interval of “run” for both groups is higher or lower, compared to the other.  This construct creates a plane for interpretation fo univariate data.  Thus, a > 1D data space - where slope vectors are vectors comprising several scalars, not just one scalar - would analogously require a 3D+ space to also include “run” for interpretation.  We generally do not do that -  we just work in the data space - but run exists in that space as a distance along the slope vector.  I like to think of shape change vectors colored blue, for example, and we can color code a portion of those blue vectors as red, corresponding to one unit of size change.  If one vector has a larger red segment than another, the distance option for comparison might reveal the two groups are different in the amount of allometric shape change.  Coloring the vectors red does nothing to change their orientation, so the angle between these vectors is a distinct test.
> > >
> > > The problem is the word, “angle”, has different meanings in the two interpretations.  I try to refrain from using “angle between slopes” for univariate data and make sure to say “different slopes” so that “angle” is a property of a multivariate space, only.  But it is confusing, nonetheless.
> > >
> > > Cheers!
> > > Mike
> > >
> > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 10:04 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Mike,
> > > >
> > > >  Whoops my bad, I just looked at the notation!
> > > >
> > > > On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 10:02, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > This was the presentation:
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Basically, I was just running a pairwise test with a single response variable, a single factor, ...
> > > > > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > As a simple demonstration, Grant could make Y a two-variable response and everything would change.
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers!
> > > > > Mike
> > > > >
> > > > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:57 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Mike and Grant,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >  Was his response a single variable? I assumed because he used Y not y in his notation,  it was a vector of multiple response variables.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 09:56, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > Ian,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Yes, the purpose seems clear, but there is not a vector of coefficients.  You have scalars b1 and b2 for two groups because there is only one variable for Y.  If b1 and b2 were vectors, you could find the distance between them and the angle between them.  As scalars, there is only a distance between them, as they exist on a line.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > In most classic univariate statistics texts/instructional sources, one might learn with ANCOVA that a pairwise comparison of slopes is performed with t = |b1 - b2|/se (using absolute values for simplicity).  That numerator is the same as the distance statistic in the RRPP pairwise summary.  The test is testing for differences between slopes, because the covariate was defined.  But slope vectors can differ in both magnitude and direction (e.g., the amount of shape change per unit size and the direction of shape change per unit size) unless there is only one variable, in which case the amount of Y change per unit size change is all one can assess.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > The only issue here is that the RRPP/pairwise function returns a result instead of alerting the user that a result like that should not be sought.  The latter is much more complicated from a programming perspective than trying to explain it in the help file, or this forum.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I hope that makes sense.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Mike
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:44 AM, Ian Dworkin <ian.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Mike (and Grant),
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  If I understand correctly what Grant is trying to achieve is to compare the angle between the vector of coefficients from the model Y ~ X2 between the groups defined by X1. i.e. like comparing the vector of coefficients from a model of shape on size for two groups (say males and females), and comparing the angle between the allometry vectors.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Let me know if I misunderstood the question.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Also we have code (probably also available in geomorph, since it seems to do everything now!) to generate CI on the angle or vector correlation via np-bootstrap. Let me know if that is useful.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Wed, 10 Jul 2019 at 09:29, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Grant,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > You are attempting to find the angle between vectors on a line.  Vectors have both a length and a direction in space with two dimensions (plane) or more, but on a line, you lose direction except for “forward” and “backward”, i.e., 0 and 180 degrees, respectively.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > It is not a strange issue with RRPP/pairwise; it’s a strange test to test the angle between vectors on a line.  The only test that can make sense is the distance between means or slopes on that line, in which case the pairwise test becomes a non-parametric form of univariate tests for pairwise differences in means or slopes, respectively.  In other words, use test.type = “dist”, only, in the summary for univariate data.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The last paragraph of the help file explains this (although a typo of test.type = ‘cor’ instead of test.type = ‘VC’ might cause some confusion - the text should still be clear about why a vector correlation does not make sense).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Mike
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Jul 10, 2019, at 9:14 AM, Grant Haines <geha...@email.wm.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Hi all,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I think I've run into a strange issue using the pairwise function in RRPP to compare angles of vectors, and I was just wondering if you had any idea of what is going on here.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Basically, I was just running a pairwise test with a single response variable, a single factor, and a continuous covariate to see how it compared to a regular ANCOVA.  I don't have a null model, because I am just interested in the angles between factor levels.  The problem is that all the angles of the group vectors were either 0º or 180º to each other, so the covariate seemed to be acting like another factor, not a continuous variable.  This isn't a huge issue in this instance because I can just use an ANCOVA, but I am also worried it is doing something similar with shape data, but it is difficult to tell since the response is multivariate.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Do you have any clue what is going on here or how to fix it?
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > The code I have is something like this:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > rrpp.df<-rrpp.data.frame(X1,X2,Y)
> > > > > > > > > > lm<-lm.rrpp(data = rrpp.df, Y~X1*X2)
> > > > > > > > > > PW<-pairwise(lm, groups = X1, covariate = X2)
> > > > > > > > > > summary(PW, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC", angle.type = "deg")
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > thanks in advance,
> > > > > > > > > > Grant

messages.subject: gpa vs bilateral symmetry
messages.body_plain:
I performed generalized Procrustes analysis on my shape data using the gpagen function. Code:

Y.gpa <- gpagen(A = avg_coords_by_species, curves= curvepts, ProcD=FALSE, Proj=TRUE)

I then enforced object symmetry on the Procrustes fit coordinates using the bilat.symmetry function. Code:

Y.sym=bilat.symmetry(Y.gpa$coords, ind = species, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = land.pairs, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 999, print.progress = TRUE)

When I plot the relationship of the PC axes (>99% of the variation) for Y.gpa$coords and Y.sym$symm.shape, there is a near linear relationship between them for the first 3 PCs. However, higher level PCs (5 through 8) are uncorrelated. Plots attached here. It is not immediately clear to me why this is the case. Can someone help me determine why the first three axes are nearly perfectly correlated but the others are not? Happy to provide more information if necessary.

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] gpa vs bilateral symmetry
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

when conducting a bilateral symmetry analysis, one of the things you obtain is the partitioning of total shape variation (from GPA) into a symmetric and asymmetric shape component. These correspond to the $sym.shape and $asym.shape parts of the output of the function. For understanding how this partitioning is done, please refer toMardia, K. V, Bookstein, F. L. & Moreton, I. J. Statistical assessment of bilateral symmetry of shapes. Biometrika 87, 285–300 (2000).

When you run a pca on Procrustes residuals (gpagen$coords), you are doing this on the total shape variation. Instead, with a pca of sym.shape you are only considering the symmetric component. This is why pca scores will never be perfectly correlated. The fact that the first pcs look highly correlated is that, in your sample (and I dare say in most biological settings), the symmetric shape component captures a large part of the total shape variation, which is reflected in the pc axes structure.

Hope this helps,

Antigoni

messages.subject: SS.type Argument for procD.pgls
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using procD.pgls to test for the strength of various ecological factors as independent variables with respect to skull shape. I am opting for SS.type III (marginal) sums of squares. For some reason, changing the value for this argument doesn't seem to actually impact the sums of squares used in the computation (no matter the value, the function always outputs results using type I SS). This is a recent issue, the argument worked normally with this exact script when I last attempted it, March 2019. Any thoughts as to what the issue could be? Am I perhaps just missing something?

Thanks,
Greg

Greg,

Try as I may, I cannot replicate your issue.  Therefore, this is what I propose as a sequence of steps to see if we can fix the problem or understand it better (don’t do all but each one in order, only moving to the next step if the previous one failed to solve the issue):

1) restart R and reload geomorph and RRPP
2) update to latest version of R and try again
3) install packages from Github via

devtools::install_github(“mlcollyer/RRPP”)
devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph”, ref = “Stable”)
 plus restart R and reload

4) Send me (not the geomorph Google group) your script and data

Also, please try to run your example with type I and type III SS and see if the values change or just the summary statement about the type of SS does not change (which maybe you have done).

Finally, check spelling.  I ran one example with SS.Type = “III” instead of SS.type = “III” and because R does not recognize the argument, it runs with the default for SS.type.  It looks like you did it correctly - just trying to find plausible reasons for your result.

Hopefully one of the earlier steps resolves the issue but if not, then we need to see if it is your computer or your data or a bug I cannot detect, by looking at your data, specifically.

Good luck!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

Does it follow from your covariance ratio papers, without the need for further simulation testing, that an appropriate statistic for the proportion of total covariance that is covariance between two shape features (blocks) is the square root of:

               CB
------------------------------        ?
sqrt(S11* x S22* x CB)

Above, CB, S11* and S22* are traces of the 'squared' cross-block, block 1, and block 2 covariance matrices, with variances zeroed out in S11 and S22 (hence *). Sorry for the ugly attempt at an equation in email text.

I'm looking for something in the spirit of an intra-class correlation coefficient, but for proportion of covariance that is between features.

Thanks for any thoughts and corrections.

David

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Repeatability of digitized landmarks calculation
messages.body_plain:
I know an intraclass correlation approach to measuring repeatability has been proposed and used for GMM studies, but I’m not sure the forced univariate concept of this coefficient yield expected results.  I’m not saying it is bad; I’m saying that one cannot necessarily have a good feeling about what the value should be in order to have “good repeatability”, as the number of landmarks should influence this score.  Fruciano et al 2016 demonstrated this to a certain extent, empirically, but it is also a concept one can realize by thinking how the alignment of landmarks must be impacted by more landmarks; i.e., the propensity for one landmark to become more variant through GPA increases with more landmarks.

Additionally, the distribution of landmarks can have huge effect.  One landmark far from the clustered others has much more leverage during GPA, and the slightest deviation is a second digitization here can have quite a shifting effect in the other landmarks, even if they were exactly placed (an artifact of GPA).

I, for one, do not like the “repeatability” assessment.  I prefer to look at the ANOVA and think about what it is telling me.  In your case,

> fit <- procD.lm(shape ~ ind + rep, data = My.df2, SS.type = "II", print.progress = FALSE)
> anova(fit)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type II
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS         MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)

ind       34 0.026502 0.00077946 0.59043 1.5514 3.7279  0.001 **
rep        1 0.001301 0.00130099 0.02898 2.5894 2.0862  0.013 *
Residuals 34 0.017083 0.00050243 0.38058
Total     69 0.044885
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ ind + rep, SS.type = "II", data = My.df2)

We learn that almost 60% of the shape variation in your sample is due to individual shape differences, about 3% seems to be from a systematic bias in the second digitization, and 38% (the ind:rep variation, which is the same as residuals) due to a combination of measurement error and GPA, combined.  does this mean a lot of measurement error?  Hard to tell, because a small error can have huge impact and a larger error can have little impact, depending on where it is isolated in the configuration.

If you are not comfortable, I would recommend two.b.pls, e.g.,

> rep1 <- My.df2$shape[,,My.df2$rep == 1]
> rep2 <- My.df2$shape[,,My.df2$rep == 2]

It could be that your individuals are so familiar that this is bound to happen.  That might be why you are thrown off with the GPA plot. messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Repeatability of digitized landmarks calculation
messages.body_plain:
As a follow up to my previous post, in case it was not clear, I once had several student digitize the same fish specimens.  When they did 5 female fish from one museum sample, it appeared measurement error was huge; when we used males and females from different samples, it was quite small.  Measurement error can only make sense in the light of variation among individuals.  Make sure the individuals you choose for a pilot study cover the range of shapes you would probably see for a full analysis.

Cheers!
Mike

> On Jul 16, 2019, at 2:52 PM, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> I know an intraclass correlation approach to measuring repeatability has been proposed and used for GMM studies, but I’m not sure the forced univariate concept of this coefficient yield expected results.  I’m not saying it is bad; I’m saying that one cannot necessarily have a good feeling about what the value should be in order to have “good repeatability”, as the number of landmarks should influence this score.  Fruciano et al 2016 demonstrated this to a certain extent, empirically, but it is also a concept one can realize by thinking how the alignment of landmarks must be impacted by more landmarks; i.e., the propensity for one landmark to become more variant through GPA increases with more landmarks.
>
> Additionally, the distribution of landmarks can have huge effect.  One landmark far from the clustered others has much more leverage during GPA, and the slightest deviation is a second digitization here can have quite a shifting effect in the other landmarks, even if they were exactly placed (an artifact of GPA).
>
> I, for one, do not like the “repeatability” assessment.  I prefer to look at the ANOVA and think about what it is telling me.  In your case,
>
> > fit <- procD.lm(shape ~ ind + rep, data = My.df2, SS.type = "II", print.progress = FALSE)
> > anova(fit)
>
> Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
> Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
> Number of permutations: 1000
> Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
> Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type II
> Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

> ind       34 0.026502 0.00077946 0.59043 1.5514 3.7279  0.001 **
> rep        1 0.001301 0.00130099 0.02898 2.5894 2.0862  0.013 *
> Residuals 34 0.017083 0.00050243 0.38058
> Total     69 0.044885

Wow, thanks Mike!
I am working on comparing different numbers of landmarks and what you mention about variation is really interesting.

I applied the above code you provided for my other landmark set using 18 landmarks and got a similar value (0.588). These specimens are from 7 populations of the same species and all female.

I then ran my code on their progeny (males and females) and got greater variation
13 landmarks
r-PLS: 0.902

P-value: 0.001

18 landmarks
r-PLS: 0.937

P-value: 0.001

I'm interpreting this as greater variation in my lab data set (2 sexes) that are allowing for a significant repeatable value between the two set of digitization, regardless of number of landmarks use (13 vs 18)?

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Repeatability of digitized landmarks calculation
messages.body_plain:
Virginia,

It does seem counter-intuitive but if one looks at the math, it makes sense.  The general interclass correlation equation is

r = Va/(Va + Vw)

for variances (V) for among (a) and within (w) components.  Notice that there will always be problems.  If individuals are really similar, Va will be small.  So even a small Vw (measurement error) might seem large.  Choose individuals that are really different, Va is large, and even a fairly large Vw could look small.

THERE IS NO GOOD WAY TO EVALUATE MEASUREMENT ERROR THIS WAY without a sense on an absolute scale what large and small is for Va and Vw, and if you knew that, you could simply measure Vw and not have to relativize Va in this way.

I think we have to remember as biologists that we are interested in detecting signals and wish to not inadvertently introduce noise (via measurement error) that could overwhelm signals.  In a pilot study, I might choose (just a couple of) individuals of different species, different sex, different sites, etc, and make 2-3 measurements per individual.  In such a case, make sure the species are quite different, maybe among sites within species not as important.  I would check to make sure that pairwise shape differences (Procrustes distances) for individuals remained consistent whether males or female, this species or that.  Maybe I learn that females are not as easy to digitize, for example.  I would compare Rsq values and I might learn that measurement error could make my females and males within sites within species hard to distinguish, but if this variation is small compared to between sites or between species, for example, then I might accept it as okay.  Finally, I would use the predict.lm.rrpp function in the RRPP package (selfish plug) to learn how resilient my estimates are despite intra-individual variability (via bootstrap resampling).  Something like this would require many digitizations per individual though, for a small sample of individuals.

In other words, assessing one’s confidence in digitization precision is much more of a process than calculating repeatability on a sample.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
David,

My initial impression is that the units of this statistic would not make sense (square root of cubed covariances in denominator).  It sounds like you would like something like Escoufier's RV coefficient (https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2307/2347233).  The RV coefficient is like a squared correlation coefficient.  Also, one can look at the singular values - like eigen values - of the cross-products between matrices.  This is not typically done with GMM data, but it is done in other areas.

Hope that helps!
Mike

> On Jul 16, 2019, at 1:02 PM, David K <katz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi there,
>
> Does it follow from your covariance ratio papers, without the need for further simulation testing, that an appropriate statistic for the proportion of total covariance that is covariance between two shape features (blocks) is the square root of:
>
>                CB
> ------------------------------        ?
> sqrt(S11* x S22* x CB)
>
> Above, CB, S11* and S22* are traces of the 'squared' cross-block, block 1, and block 2 covariance matrices, with variances zeroed out in S11 and S22 (hence *). Sorry for the ugly attempt at an equation in email text.
>
> I'm looking for something in the spirit of an intra-class correlation coefficient, but for proportion of covariance that is between features.
>
> Thanks for any thoughts and corrections.
>
> David

messages.body_plain:
Mike,

Thanks for your response. This wouldn't quite work for what I'd like to quantify. First, RV incorporates trait variances in the denominator components. Beyond that, unless I am misunderstanding something, RV and CR are  proportions of between-to-within block magnitudes (differing by whether one takes a square root of the proportion).

I have in mind that there is a total amount covariance in a sample/system, and I'd like to know what percentage of it is covariance between pre-defined blocks of traits.

David

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Proportion of total covariance that is between blocks
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Proportion of total covariance that is between blocks
messages.body_plain:
David,

This is difficult concept to approach.  I realize you do not wish to have variances in the denominator but to measure a percentage of covariation, one would need to have a measure of possible 100% covariation.  What would that be?  If you think about the Pearson correlation coefficient - cov(x,y) / sqrt(Vx * Vy), where V means variance, the denominator is the maximum possible covariance, found from the product of variances.  The RV coefficient is a squared multivariate generalization of this.

Here is another way to think about it.  Both the RV and CR have the same numerator part: trace(X’YY'X), where X and Y are mean-centered and ‘ means the matrix is transposed.  (There is no need to worry about degrees of freedom - they cancel out in the numerator and denominator.)  This product is the amount of squared covariance between X and Y blocks.  How could it be maximized?  When X = Y is one way.  Then the denominator of the RV, which is the square root of trace(X’XX’X) * trace(Y’YY’Y), is the same as the square root of trace(X’YY’X) * trace(Y’XX’Y), which just happens to be the same as the square root of the square of the numerator.  I just point this out to illustrate that - only in this case of equality - that the former finds sums of squares (variances if divided by degrees of freedom) along the diagonal of X’X or Y’Y but the latter does not.  Therefore, in finding the maximum covariation possible, I’m not sure that having variances in the calculations presents some kind of insurmountable challenge.

However, there are many issues with the RV and its concept of generalization to argue.  One that bothers me is that the numerator finds the trace of a cross-product of matrix cross-products (crazy enough on its own) and the denominator finds two traces of crossproducts and multiplies them, as if this is fair.  (Makes no sense to me.)  So I am in no way advocating RV, but it is a multivariate version of measuring the amount of covariation as a proportion of the total possible.

You mentioned intraclass correlation.  One could do that with CRnum/(CRdenom + CRnum) where num and denom are the numerator and denominator parts of the squared CR statistic, respectively (the CR without the square root over all of it).  I suppose there is theoretical limit where CR denom approaches 0, CR approaches infinity, and an intraclass correlation approaches 1 (although this is difficult to perceive).  I simply have no idea how such a statistic would behave under null conditions, but one could simulate that and assess whether it behaves as it should (random data should not produce strong correlations)

If it were me, I would simply do a singular value decomposition of the cross-covariance matrix and look at the distribution of singular values.  I cannot think of a good way to improve on that.  If the variables are standardized, then the sum of singular values has a maximum of p^2, for p variables.  The sum of singular values divided by p^2 might be a possible way to measure the amount of covariation, but this might be quite similar to RV.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Mike. I've started playing around with some simulations and will let you know if anything interesting comes of it. Someone pointed out to me years ago that the Pearson's coefficient denominator was a maximum covariance, but I'd completely forgotten about it. It's a useful perspective to be reminded of in this case.

On Wed, Jul 17, 2019 at 5:10 AM Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> David,
>
> This is difficult concept to approach.  I realize you do not wish to have variances in the denominator but to measure a percentage of covariation, one would need to have a measure of possible 100% covariation.  What would that be?  If you think about the Pearson correlation coefficient - cov(x,y) / sqrt(Vx * Vy), where V means variance, the denominator is the maximum possible covariance, found from the product of variances.  The RV coefficient is a squared multivariate generalization of this.
>
> Here is another way to think about it.  Both the RV and CR have the same numerator part: trace(X’YY'X), where X and Y are mean-centered and ‘ means the matrix is transposed.  (There is no need to worry about degrees of freedom - they cancel out in the numerator and denominator.)  This product is the amount of squared covariance between X and Y blocks.  How could it be maximized?  When X = Y is one way.  Then the denominator of the RV, which is the square root of trace(X’XX’X) * trace(Y’YY’Y), is the same as the square root of trace(X’YY’X) * trace(Y’XX’Y), which just happens to be the same as the square root of the square of the numerator.  I just point this out to illustrate that - only in this case of equality - that the former finds sums of squares (variances if divided by degrees of freedom) along the diagonal of X’X or Y’Y but the latter does not.  Therefore, in finding the maximum covariation possible, I’m not sure that having variances in the calculations presents some kind of insurmountable challenge.
>
> However, there are many issues with the RV and its concept of generalization to argue.  One that bothers me is that the numerator finds the trace of a cross-product of matrix cross-products (crazy enough on its own) and the denominator finds two traces of crossproducts and multiplies them, as if this is fair.  (Makes no sense to me.)  So I am in no way advocating RV, but it is a multivariate version of measuring the amount of covariation as a proportion of the total possible.
>
> You mentioned intraclass correlation.  One could do that with CRnum/(CRdenom + CRnum) where num and denom are the numerator and denominator parts of the squared CR statistic, respectively (the CR without the square root over all of it).  I suppose there is theoretical limit where CR denom approaches 0, CR approaches infinity, and an intraclass correlation approaches 1 (although this is difficult to perceive).  I simply have no idea how such a statistic would behave under null conditions, but one could simulate that and assess whether it behaves as it should (random data should not produce strong correlations)
>
> If it were me, I would simply do a singular value decomposition of the cross-covariance matrix and look at the distribution of singular values.  I cannot think of a good way to improve on that.  If the variables are standardized, then the sum of singular values has a maximum of p^2, for p variables.  The sum of singular values divided by p^2 might be a possible way to measure the amount of covariation, but this might be quite similar to RV.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike
>
> > On Jul 16, 2019, at 7:16 PM, David K <katz...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Mike,
> >
> > Thanks for your response. This wouldn't quite work for what I'd like to quantify. First, RV incorporates trait variances in the denominator components. Beyond that, unless I am misunderstanding something, RV and CR are  proportions of between-to-within block magnitudes (differing by whether one takes a square root of the proportion).
> >
> > I have in mind that there is a total amount covariance in a sample/system, and I'd like to know what percentage of it is covariance between pre-defined blocks of traits.
> >
> > David
> >
> > On Tue, Jul 16, 2019 at 4:00 PM Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > David,
> > >
> > > My initial impression is that the units of this statistic would not make sense (square root of cubed covariances in denominator).  It sounds like you would like something like Escoufier's RV coefficient (https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2307/2347233).  The RV coefficient is like a squared correlation coefficient.  Also, one can look at the singular values - like eigen values - of the cross-products between matrices.  This is not typically done with GMM data, but it is done in other areas.
> > >
> > > Hope that helps!
> > > Mike
> > >
> > > > On Jul 16, 2019, at 1:02 PM, David K <katz...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi there,
> > > >
> > > > Does it follow from your covariance ratio papers, without the need for further simulation testing, that an appropriate statistic for the proportion of total covariance that is covariance between two shape features (blocks) is the square root of:
> > > >
> > > >                CB
> > > > ------------------------------        ?
> > > > sqrt(S11* x S22* x CB)
> > > >
> > > > Above, CB, S11* and S22* are traces of the 'squared' cross-block, block 1, and block 2 covariance matrices, with variances zeroed out in S11 and S22 (hence *). Sorry for the ugly attempt at an equation in email text.
> > > >
> > > > I'm looking for something in the spirit of an intra-class correlation coefficient, but for proportion of covariance that is between features.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for any thoughts and corrections.
> > > >
> > > > David

Peter,

There are no functional errors. The apparent 50% arrest is just a screen-printing glitch. I’ll have to look into what is causing that. The other messages are warnings, not errors, because your model design matrix has too many columns (probably because you do not have all levels of one factor interacting with all levels of the other). Rather than arrest the analysis, QR decomposition is used to adjust the model design matrix, which is why the warning appears. Without the warning, one might wonder why degrees of freedom change in ANOVA.

Hope that is clear.

Mike

messages.subject: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses
messages.subject_clean: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am running both PGLS (procD.pgls) and PPLS (phylo.integration) analyses to test for the significance of ecology as a predictor of skull shape in snakes. For procD.pgls, categorical ecological variables were used as the independent variables (i.e. all species with landmark data were categorically coded as arboreal, terrestrial etc., diurnal, nocturnal, etc., diet as amphibians, reptiles, etc.). For the PPLS analysis, quantitative diet data, (a matrix of proportions of each type of prey consumed), was used for the second block. Separate analyses were run for each of 8 snake skull elements (i.e. 8 different landmark subsets), and the ecological variables were found to be significant predictors of shape in all but a couple of cases (across all landmark subsets and ecological variables).

This seemed like a red flag to me, so I proceeded to randomly permute my ecological data, creating 1000 random ecological datasets. I then re-ran the analyses and found that I am getting significant results far more often than I should be with the randomly permuted datasets (between 40-70% of the time depending on the landmark subset and ecological variable in question, α=0.05, n=1000) for both PGLS and PPLS analyses. I am not sure what could possibly be driving this or if there is simply something I am missing in the usage of these functions.

I would really appreciate any thoughts or explanations as to what may be going on here.

Thanks,
Greg

Here is an example portion of the script I used to run the analyses:

# Landmarks aligned prior to this

# Loading categorical data for habitat use, temporal activity, and major diet category from csv file (for PGLS analysis)

Ecological_Data<-read.csv("Ecological_Data.csv", row.names=1)

# Loading quantitative data for diet proportions (for PPLS analysis)

Quantitative_Diet<-read.csv("Diet_Quantitative_Proportions.csv", row.names=1)

# Tree for PGLS

Zaher_tree<-read.tree("Zaher_2019_Phylogeny_SpeciesLandmarked")

# Tree for PPLS

Zaher_tree_PPLS<-keep.tip(Zaher_tree, diet_labels)

# Creating data frame for subsequent PGLS analyses

Zaher_notroph<-geomorph.data.frame(coords=aligned_notroph_phylo, Habitat_Use=Ecological_Data[,1], Activity=Ecological_Data[,2], Diet=Ecological_Data[,3], phy=Zaher_tree)

# PPLS Analysis for Non-Trophic Landmark Subset

phylo.integration(A=aligned_notroph_diet, A2=Quantitative_Diet, Zaher_tree_PPLS)

# PGLS Analysis for Non-Trophic Landmark Subset

summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Habitat_Use+Activity+Diet, phy=phy, data=Zaher_notroph, SS.type="III"))

Hello,

To append some additional information to my original question, I should also mention that r-squared valued when running the PGLS test have been behaving strangely. With my original dataset of ~110 species, procD.pgls was returning very homogenous r-squared values in the ballpark of 0.1-0.15 for every independent variable across all 8 skull elements (landmark subsets) separately analyzed. After increasing my dataset to its current size of 160 species, procD.pgls returned r-squared values that were either very high (~0.8) or very low (~0.02), with no intermediate values, across all three independent variables and across all landmark subsets.

I recently ran another randomization test with the goal of determining what the r-squared values would look like with randomized ecological data (done in the same way as when I did this for significance values above). I've attached some rough plots of what the r-squared values are looking like with randomized ecological data (for each of the three independent variables) over the course of 100 iterations of the randomization test. Strangely, the values seem to gravitate towards either ~0.8 or ~0.02, the same values I was seeing with my original, non-randomized data.

I have talked to a couple of people in my lab about this, as well as my advisor, and they were baffled as to what the issue could be. I would really appreciate any thoughts folks might have.

Thanks,
Greg

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Re: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Re: Significance in PGLS and PPLS Analyses
messages.body_plain:
Greg,

It is impossible to know what is going on with your particular dataset from the descriptions so far. One comment I will make however is that your randomization approach is not a formal test of the method itself, nor does it necessarily reveal a pathology. For this, one must generate actual random data under a null model with a known pattern (read: permuting data will still have the peculiarities of those data in them: they are not necessarily examples of ‘null random’ pattern!). Thus, such evaluations are more apt to reveal curiosities of a particular data set and/or phylogeny rather than the method itself.

Without knowing more on what your data have and what you have done with them, I can only remind folks that the behavior for any particular dataset also depends on how the categorical variable is distributed on the phylogeny. We investigated this for phylogenetic anova last year and found that the extent to which the factor levels of the categorical variable ‘associate’ with phylogenetic clusters of taxa (ie subclades) can have a substantial effect on downstream phylogenetic anova (see Adams and Collyer 2018: Evolution).  This is not a problem with phylogenetic anova per se, but rather an unappreciated fact of the extent to which the categorical variable displays phylogenetic signal. We propose a means of investigating this in the paper via PLS.

For your particular example, it is impossible to know whether this is resulting in outcomes that you do not expect (though where the expectations come from is also something to consider). Regardless, I suggest you investigate this a bit more as per above to see the extent to which this provides insight.

I hope I’ve understood your question(s) sufficiently to point you in a good direction. If not, please let me know off-line and I can try to find time to discuss some more.

Best,

Dean

Juan,

That is certainly not a huge number of species for such a comparison. The algebra will ‘work’, but I’d be very cautious with my interpretation, regardless of the method used to assess significance.

I suspect that you have many more variables than sample size (N = 8); meaning that your data do not occupy or ‘fill up’ the morphospace very well. Thus, spurious statistical results are likely. This may be one reason why results differ under simulation versus permutation. For the latter, it uses the same 8 shapes re-assigned to different branches of the tree for testing significance. Whereas for the former, the method simulates data under Brownian motion, and across many runs it may investigate more components of morphospace than your original 8 specimens; thereby leading to a result that states the groups are not overly different as compared to a random selection of phenotypes in morphospace.  When interpreting such patterns I tend to be more conservative, and state up-front the caveats of my dataset (in this case, a small number of specimens relative to variables).

Of course, something we always advocate is an investigation of the effect size of any statistical test: not just reliance on p-values. If the effect size is quite large, then this provides important information for interpreting the patterns biologically. Mike and I have discussed this at length in this forum in previous posts: whether it be for interpreting linear model effects, modularity / integration signal, or results from phylogenetic comparative methods. I recommend that here also.

Good luck!

When confronted with an error like yours - one that arises without any package updates - my course of action is this:

1. Restart R.  If this does not work,
2. Restart computer and restart R.  If this does not work,
3. Reinstall R (and R studio) and relaunch.  If this does not work,
4. Make sure to update all packages that could be at fault (geomorph, RRPP, and dependencies).  If that does not work,
5. Debug

The debug part is the geomorph and RRPP teams' responsibility, so if the first four fail, then let us know.

The type of error you received is unusual.  It makes me suspect that R is having a seizure.  When R has a seizure, updating R might be needed.

messages.subject: Re: Explanation for bilat.symmetry results
messages.body_plain:
Dear Rochishnu,

You've gotten two ANOVA tables. First relates to shape analysis. It is Procrustes ANOVA table. Here You can see significant effects of individual (there is inter-individual variation in shape), side (ther is a directional asymmetry of shape), and individual to side interaction (there is a significant fluctuating asymmetry, this means that fluctuating asymmetry is more than measurement error in Your data). The second table is analoguous but relates to the analysis of size. There are no significant effects.

You can consult with papers by Klingenberg for more explanation.

Klingenberg C.P., McIntyre G.S. Geometric Morphometrics of Developmental Instability: Analyzing Patterns of Fluctuating Asymmetry with Procrustes Methods // Evolution. 1998. 52. I. 5. 1363–1375.
Klingenberg C.P., Barluenga M., Meyer A. Shape Analysis of Symmetric Structures: Quantifying Variation Among Individuals and Asymmetry // Evolution. 2002. 56. I. 10. 1909–1920.

Hope this helps.

Best regards,
Basil Yakimov

Here You can see significant effects of individual (there is inter-individual variation in shape), side (ther is a directional asymmetry of shape), and individual to side interaction (there is a significant fluctuating asymmetry, this means that fluctuating asymmetry is more than measurement error in Your data). The second table is analoguous but relates to the analysis of size. There are no significant effects.

You can consult with papers by Klingenberg for more explanation.

Klingenberg C.P., McIntyre G.S. Geometric Morphometrics of Developmental Instability: Analyzing Patterns of Fluctuating Asymmetry with Procrustes Methods // Evolution. 1998. 52. I. 5. 1363–1375.

Klingenberg C.P., Barluenga M., Meyer A. Shape Analysis of Symmetric Structures: Quantifying Variation Among Individuals and Asymmetry // Evolution. 2002. 56. I. 10. 1909–1920.

Hope this helps.

Best regards,

Basil Yakimov

messages.subject: Correct modularity.test set up
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was wondering if I could get your input on my modularity.test set up?

I’m interested in testing whether the opercular four-bar lever (OFB) and pelvic girdle complex (PGC) are modules within my dataset. I had originally partitioned the OFB (made up of 33 landmarks) and tested it against the remainder of the skeletal shape (101 landmarks), and then run a second analysis looking at the PGC (made up of 22 landmarks) against the remainder of the skeletal shape (112 landmarks).

Can I test for modularity in this manner (ie OFB-Total), or do I need to pick another hypothetical module in the skull to test against? Should I continue to run the OFB and PGC as separate modularity tests, or is there another way to address this? In addition, if testing the OFB and PGC against the total skeleton is valid, would randomly subsampling the ‘total’ partition to a similar number of landmarks as the OFB or PGC partitions be more appropriate for this test? I realize I may have misread Adams (2016) in regards to number of variables, as I believe having different numbers of landmarks within each partition (OFB-Total or PGC-Total) may be skewing my results.

Thank you very much in advance,

Tegan

messages.body_plain:
Tegan,

I don’t think I mentioned that a difference in landmarks affects the results using the covariance ratio.

As to your procedural questions (ie, which modules to investigate), that is a hypothesis-related issue. One can examine the degree of modularity in a hypothesis containing modules A vs. B, or B’ vs. C, or A vs B vs. C. This last one reminds users that one can use the CR coefficient on objects with more than 2 modules; it need not be an either-or type analysis for pairs of hypothesized modules only.

Hope this helps.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Correct modularity.test set up
messages.body_plain:
David,

That is an interesting philosophical question, but one whose alternatives are quite hard to distinguish mathematically. In fact, I assert that for 2 putative modules, they are indistinguishable. Here is why.

Using the current modularity measures (e.g., the CR, RV, and even the EMMLi approach), patterns of modularity are defined in relative terms; where the covariation between modules is characterized RELATIVE to the covariation within modules. So then, what is the expected pattern if A and B are ‘good’ modules, versus where A is a module and B is not? I simply do not know. Put another way, if there are only two ‘groups’ of variables, I don’t think there is actually a mathematical difference between A & B as modules or just A as a module. Both would show some smaller between-module covariation, as at least A is a ‘good’ module.

Now, if there are 3 putative modules, then one can distinguish the patterns a bit better. For instance, one could have A & B & C as ‘good’ modules, but an alternative where A is a ‘good’ module, but B & C are not.  In the latter case. B & C are indistinguishable, meaning there is effectively a pattern of: A vs (B,C).   This is now the difference between a 2-module hypothesis and a 3-module hypothesis.

Here one has something to examine; namely, one can compare the strength of signal in a 2- vs a 3-module hypothesis and determine which as the stronger support.  Currently geomorph does not implement this. However, we have a method in review precisely for this purpose. Once it is accepted we will release the approach in geomorph, as we feel this is a useful extension of the current modularity toolkit.

Dean
